title: Automotive Parts & Accessories Association, Inc. v. Boyd
lead: Accessory sellers support head restraints but challenge a rule requiring them in new cars; the court asks whether informal procedure still supplied adequate reasons and support.

actors.name: Sterling Products and accessory trade associations
actors.role: Aftermarket interests challenging factory installation; ASIA intervened.

actors.name: Transportation authorities and Federal Highway Administrator
actors.role: Officials issuing Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 202.

proceedings: The agency adopted the standard in February 1968 and denied reconsideration in May.
Accessory interests petitioned directly for review in consolidated D.C. Circuit proceedings.
The unanimous panel denied review on December 27, 1968.
limits: The court reached the formal-hearing argument despite a preservation concern and reached alternative merits on petitioners’ changed safety argument. It reserved the asserted lack of power to mandate consumer installation under an equipment standard.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The agency chooses a vehicle requirement after successive proposals
paragraphs: Under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, transportation authorities proposed twenty-three standards in November 1966 and issued twenty in January 1967. They withheld head restraints for more study, sought comments, and met interested manufacturers and others in November 1967. A revised proposal in December accepted comments through January 26, 1968. The final Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 202 issued February 12, incorporating some suggestions but rejecting the accessory industry’s preferred approach.

Effective January 1, 1969, new passenger cars manufactured for United States sale had to include factory-installed front-seat head restraints meeting federal requirements. A vehicle standard controlled the car as manufactured for sale; an equipment standard governed an accessory without necessarily assuring installation in every car.

Sterling Products and the Automotive Parts & Accessories Association challenged the choice, and the other trade association identified as ASIA intervened in consolidated review. They were accessory interests, not the automobile manufacturers. They had supported head restraints’ safety value but feared lost aftermarket sales. The agency denied reconsideration in a reasoned three-page letter on May 20, 1968.

sections.title: The accessory interests propose certified add-ons and formal hearings
sections.cue: What choices and objections did the agency confront?
paragraphs: The challengers wanted certified accessory products so buyers could choose brand and fit, with installation before delivery if mandatory. They argued factory requirements increased price and industry concentration, slowed improvements, encouraged minimum designs, reduced choice, and delayed protection that cheap, easy add-ons could deliver sooner. The agency responded that optional equipment would not guarantee installation, restraint performance depended on seats and anchorage, and vehicle standards allowed both integral-seat and add-on designs.

In direct court review they also demanded formal Administrative Procedure Act hearings. They had not raised that objection during rulemaking or reconsideration. Judge McGowan’s unanimous panel identified serious preservation concerns but decided the question because the Government defended the merits and administration of the new law involved a public interest. The result was not a waiver holding.

Formal §§ 556–557 procedures attach under § 553 when a statute requires rules on the record after an agency hearing. The Safety Act generally applied the APA to standards but did not impose that requirement. Calling standards “orders” did not turn future general policy into adjudication. Senate language excluded formal procedures; the House version and report permitted choice; conference adopted that version, and Senator Magnuson explained formal process was optional. Research, consultation, and experimentation fit informal policy formation.

sections.title: An informal record can support searching review
sections.cue: Why did review provisions not silently create a trial requirement?
paragraphs: Petitioners argued that filing the agency record in court, judicial review, and remand for more evidence required a formal evidentiary hearing. McGowan disagreed. Comments and other rulemaking materials made a record capable of supplementation. Review did not override statutory history and structure.

Section 706(2)(E)’s substantial-evidence provision applied to the formal proceedings its text identified, not automatically whenever this statute authorized review. Other § 706 grounds still permitted searching, strict examination of appropriate legislative materials. The opinion’s later description of substantial support did not change the proceeding’s legal review standard.

APA § 553(c) also required a concise general statement of basis and purpose. The short promulgation statement identified neck-injury reduction, but the court considered it with the agency’s promulgation explanation and reconsideration letter. Note 12 expressly made the latter relevant. The Court did not approve a bare purpose sentence as universally enough. Reasons need not address every submission or make formal findings on every issue, but must expose major policy choices and why they were made. Judges should not have to construct rationale by searching the record themselves.

sections.title: The agency explains why complete vehicles better protect occupants
sections.cue: What supported the rejected alternatives and implementation date?
paragraphs: The agency connected universal installation and enforceability with engineering evidence about restraint, seat, and anchorage. It explained performance-standard design flexibility and why safety outweighed accessory sellers’ disadvantage. These were contemporaneous agency reasons supplied through promulgation and reconsideration, not new litigation rationalizations.

The court found conscientious consideration and supported rejection of the alternatives. Expert evidence supported structural integration, and the record supported January 1, 1969 implementation. The proposed faster optional model would reduce assured protection. Although the Administrator also claimed no statutory power to force purchasers to install equipment after an equipment-only standard, the court expressly reserved that legal question because other grounds sufficed.

In court petitioners changed position to argue restraints were unnecessary or hazardous, relying on automobile manufacturers’ submissions despite those manufacturers not challenging the final rule. McGowan criticized the inconsistency with their earlier support and demand for speed but also decided the merits alternatively. Independent research, medical evidence, and departmental statistics supported fewer neck injuries in rear-end crashes; visibility and other asserted harms were speculative. The agency could reasonably weigh the consequences.

The standard met practicability, safety need, and objective-term requirements with attention to data, consultation, vehicle suitability, and statutory purpose. Economic loss did not defeat this supported safety judgment. That conclusion was neither an antitrust adjudication nor a rule that any safety assertion overrides every economic objection.

sections.title: Organization and consultation objections also fail
sections.cue: What remained in force after the petitions were denied?
paragraphs: The court rejected the claim that the wrong official acted. Transportation statutes, organization, and delegations permitted the Federal Highway Administrator’s exercise of authority, and the bureau director participated in research, consultation, and reports. The director had not been unlawfully bypassed.

The advisory council needed a general-public majority, not a representative from every private-interest category. The record supported consultation with both it and the Vehicle Equipment Safety Commission. Those findings concerned this organizational framework and record.

On December 27, 1968, Chief Judge Bazelon and Judges McGowan and Robinson unanimously denied the petitions, leaving Standard No. 202 operative. No district-court judgment or damages award existed to affirm. Informal rulemaking was permissible, its major choices adequately explained, and its policy supported; each was a separate necessary inquiry. The account concerns the historical standard, not present vehicle requirements.
